How likely are we to have an economic breakdown in two years?
Predictions like these are made all the time. The sky is, in all likelihood, not falling. ...yet.

Everyone is pointing to September because of the financial market downturn that seems to happen every 7 years. One of the biggest problems is that it can turn into a self fulfilling prophecy if a majority of people do in fact take their money out of financial markets because they think a September downturn is going to happen.

With that said, US equities are way over valued. The Fed has kept interest rates way too low for way too long. China appears to be dumping US Treasuries. The housing market for a lot of areas is over valued because the banks won't let the market clear. The official unemployment numbers are a joke, real unemployment number is around 20%. From what I can tell, a lot of emerging market currency's are depreciating against the dollar, this can be either good or bad depending on what side of the fence you're on.

So yeah, you've got a lot of negatives going on right now. Is everything going to collapse in September? Fuck if I know.

Bear in mind I'm no economist but... It depends where you look and who you believe. In fact it depends on your definition of economic breakdown too. If we're talking about something on the scale of the banking crash of 2008 I'd say it's quite likely, but if we're talking great depression of the 1930s in Germany I'd say it's very unlikely.

The price of oil is getting lower and lower, this affects all sectors and influences the markets heavily. The economy is all but linked to oil nowadays rather than gold as it was before, so any major changes in the price of oil will have a big impact. China's economy could also cause major headaches for the world economy if it doesn't stabilise soon. The EU could cause the world economy to stumble if member countries like Greece keep having problems.

Realistically, the world economy is a complex piece of machinery with a lot of moving parts that all depend on each other. One part snaps and suddenly it could be in need of repairs.

97% of new money is created through private banks primarily in the form of debt. (PDF)

The vast majority of people don't understand how money is created in today's economy. They somehow think the Fed or somebody just prints it out and somehow that just kind of ends up in circulation. In reality 'printed' money only accounts for about 3% of new money. In reality money is primarily created by common banks. They're allowed to lend on margin - that's the entire premise of fractional reserve banking. You open up BankUSA. You get your first depositor Joe who gives you $100. You're now legally allowed in the US to lend out $90. If Joe comes back for his money you don't have it - that's where the central bank or Fed comes to save the day.

This doesn't sound so bad until you think about what actually happens. That $90 you lent out is now going to get spent or invested and ultimately deposited at another (or perhaps even the same) bank. Well you get a $90 deposit - you lend out $81. This process keeps getting repeated. What ultimately happens if you work out the math is that $100 of deposits turns int $1000 of debt. And it's not just that. Banks are allowed to charge interest on their loans, even when they don't actually have enough money to cover the loans. So a $100 deposit becomes $1000 of debt and potentially thousands of more dollars in interest of debt. Each $100 of real money ends up with the potential of creating thousands of dollars of debt that is in no way backed by 'real' money. How do people pay off this debt? With money from other people that's also going to be debt. Then they deposit it and the banks lend it out creating even more exponential levels of debt.

Our entire economy is like a roller coaster that has to accelerate faster and faster to keep from falling off the tracks. This one reason the Fed is freaking out about not being able to keep inflation rising. It means people aren't spending which is another way of saying that roller coaster is suddenly starting to stutter. Inflation encourages investment since otherwise your money effectively just rots away. It's also obviously a sign of spending.
